chunks: Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Abū Isḥāq al-Nahāwandī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Barqī, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from a man whom he mentioned, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:

I said to him: We are sometimes on the road to Makkah intending ihram, and we do not have with us bran with which we rub ourselves after using depilatory lime, so we rub ourselves with flour, and because of that something enters my mind of which Allah knows best. He said: "Out of fear of extravagance in using it?" I said: Yes. He said: "There is no extravagance in what benefits and restores the body. I myself have at times ordered fine flour to be moistened with oil, then I rub myself with it; extravagance is only in that which wastes wealth and harms the body."
I saw Abā Jaʿfar al-Thānī عليه السلام come out of the bathhouse, and from the top of his head to his feet he was like a rose from the effect of henna.

key_terms.الدَّقِيقِ: flour used here as a substitute for bodily rubbing
key_terms.النُّورَةِ: depilatory lime used to remove hair
key_terms.الْإِحْرَامَ: the state of consecration entered for hajj or ʿumrah
key_terms.الْحِنَّاءِ: henna, whose effect appeared on the body
key_terms.نُخَالَةٌ: bran used here for rubbing the body after depilatory treatment

ai.seo_question: Is using flour for bodily care before ihram considered extravagance in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith explains that using flour for bodily care in preparation for ihram is not considered extravagance when it serves a beneficial bodily purpose. It defines true extravagance as that which wastes wealth and harms the body, and it also reports an observation of Abū Jaʿfar al-Thānī عليه السلام after leaving the bathhouse with the visible effect of henna.
